lit-u4-l1: A student fails every subject and his friend says, 'Wow, you are a genius!' What device is this?
Verbal irony
Dramatic irony
Simile
Hyperbole
The friend says the opposite of what he means. That is verbal irony.
Does the friend really think he is a genius?
Verbal irony is when:
A speaker says the opposite of what they really mean
The audience knows something a character does not
Events turn out the opposite of what was expected
A character speaks alone on stage
Verbal irony lies in the gap between the words and the speaker's real meaning.
Focus on what a character SAYS.
Sarcasm is best described as:
Bitter or mocking verbal irony meant to hurt or criticise
A kind of rhyme
A friendly compliment
A sound device
Sarcasm is a sharp, mocking form of verbal irony.
Is sarcasm kind or cutting?
During heavy rain, a man soaked to the skin says, 'Lovely weather for a picnic!' The tone is:
Sarcastic
Joyful
Sorrowful
Fearful
He means the weather is terrible, so his words are sarcastic verbal irony.
Is the weather good for a picnic?
Which sentence contains verbal irony?
After NEPA took light for the fifth time, Bisi said, 'Great service, as usual!'
Bisi said the light had gone off.
Bisi was angry because the light went off.
The light went off like a blown candle.
Bisi praises the service while meaning it is terrible. That is verbal irony.
Find the sentence where the words don't match the real meaning.
How can a reader recognise verbal irony in a text?
The words clash with the situation or the speaker's known feelings
The sentence uses 'like' or 'as'
The line rhymes with the next
The speaker uses many sound words
Irony is spotted when what is said contrasts with what we know is true.
Compare what is said with what is actually happening.
A teacher sees a student arrive two hours late and says, 'Thank you for joining us so early.' What is the teacher really saying?
The student is very late
The student is early
The student is welcome any time
The class has not started
'So early' means the opposite here. The teacher is pointing out that the student is late.
Is two hours late early?
Understatement used for ironic effect, like calling a burnt house 'a little damaged', is called:
Litotes or ironic understatement
Hyperbole
Personification
Onomatopoeia
Playing down something serious creates ironic understatement.
Is the speaker exaggerating or playing it down?
Why do writers use verbal irony?
To create humour, criticise, or show a character's attitude
To give exact information
To describe sounds
To make lines rhyme
Irony can amuse, criticise indirectly, or reveal what a character thinks.
What effect does saying the opposite have?
lit-u4-l2: Situational irony occurs when:
What happens is the opposite of what was expected
A speaker says the opposite of what he means
The audience knows more than the characters
Two opposite words are joined
Situational irony is about events: the outcome contradicts expectations.
Is it about words or about events?
A fire station burns down. Why is this ironic?
A place meant to fight fires is destroyed by fire
Fires are dangerous
Fire stations are expensive
It happened at night
We expect a fire station to stop fires, not suffer one. The contradiction is situational irony.
What is a fire station supposed to do?
A man works all his life to send his son abroad, but the son returns and becomes a farmer in the same village. This is:
Situational irony
Verbal irony
Dramatic irony
Sarcasm
The father's effort leads to the very result he tried to avoid. That is situational irony.
Did things turn out as the father expected?
Which of these is an example of situational irony?
A traffic warden gets a fine for illegal parking
A student passes an exam after studying
A farmer harvests yams in the rainy season
A teacher marks a test
We expect a traffic warden to enforce parking rules, not break them.
Which result is the opposite of what you expect?
A villager boasts that no thief can enter his house, and that same night he is robbed. This irony mainly creates:
A sense of humbling surprise and a lesson about pride
A romantic mood
Confusion about the plot
A sound effect
His proud boast is followed by the opposite outcome, which teaches a lesson about pride.
What does the outcome do to his boast?
A swimming instructor drowns in a bathtub. The irony comes from:
The contrast between his skill and his fate
The size of the bathtub
The time of the accident
His being a teacher
An expert swimmer drowning in shallow water is the opposite of what we expect.
What would you expect of a swimming instructor?
In a novel, a corrupt chief pays a herbalist to destroy his rival, but the charm kills the chief instead. This is an example of:
Situational irony
Dramatic monologue
Comic relief
Foreshadowing
His plot backfires on him, the opposite of what he planned.
Who was supposed to be harmed?
How is situational irony different from dramatic irony?
Situational irony is about unexpected outcomes; dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than the characters
They are exactly the same
Situational irony is about words; dramatic irony is about sounds
Dramatic irony only happens in poems
Situational irony concerns how events turn out. Dramatic irony concerns what the audience knows.
One is about outcomes, the other about knowledge.
A doctor who always warns patients against smoking is seen smoking outside the hospital. Why is this ironic?
His behaviour contradicts the advice he gives
Doctors work long hours
Hospitals are busy
Smoking is legal
We expect the doctor to follow his own advice. His action is the opposite.
What do we expect from someone who gives advice?
lit-u4-l3: Dramatic irony occurs when:
The audience knows something that a character does not
A character says the opposite of what he means
The ending is happy
The play has no dialogue
In dramatic irony, the audience's knowledge is greater than a character's.
Who knows more, the audience or the character?
In a play, the audience knows the drink is poisoned, but the king happily raises his cup. What does this create?
Tension and suspense through dramatic irony
Comic relief
A soliloquy
Verbal irony
Because we know the danger and he doesn't, we feel tension. That is dramatic irony.
Why are we nervous watching him drink?
Why do playwrights use dramatic irony?
To build suspense and involve the audience emotionally
To confuse the audience
To end the play quickly
To replace dialogue
Knowing more than the characters makes the audience anxious and involved.
How do you feel when you know something a character doesn't?
In Ola Rotimi's The Gods Are Not to Blame, the audience knows Odewale has married his own mother long before he does. This is:
Dramatic irony
Verbal irony
Situational irony only
Comic relief
The audience knows the terrible truth while Odewale is still ignorant of it. That is dramatic irony.
Who knows the truth first?
A character says, 'I trust my friend completely,' while the audience has just watched the friend plotting to betray him. The effect is:
The audience feels pity and dread for the character
The audience laughs at the friend
The audience is bored
The audience forgets the plot
His innocent trust, set against what we know, creates pity and dread.
What do you want to shout at him?
Which of these is an example of dramatic irony?
Viewers know a surprise party is waiting, but the birthday girl thinks everyone forgot her
A man says 'nice weather' in a storm
A fire station burns down
Two drunk guards argue about wine
The audience knows about the party while the character does not.
Which option has a gap between what the audience and the character know?
Dramatic irony is especially powerful in tragedy because:
The audience watches the hero move towards a disaster he cannot see
Tragedies are always funny
The hero always wins
Tragedies have no audience
Knowing the doom ahead while the hero walks into it creates deep pity and fear.
What does the audience see coming?
In a Nollywood film, the viewer sees the house girl stealing money, while the madam blames her son. The viewer's knowledge creates:
Dramatic irony
Onomatopoeia
A soliloquy
Metonymy
We know the real thief, but the madam does not.
Who knows the truth?
What must a student explain when discussing dramatic irony in an exam?
What the audience knows, what the character does not know, and the effect
Only the name of the playwright
The rhyme scheme
The number of acts in the play
Explain the gap in knowledge and how it affects the audience.
Name the gap and its effect.
lit-u4-l4: Satire is a form of writing that:
Uses humour or irony to criticise people or society
Satire mocks foolishness or wrongdoing in order to criticise and correct.
Why would a writer make fun of a corrupt leader?
The main purpose of satire is to:
Expose and correct faults in society
Satire ridicules vices so that society may see them and change.
What does satire hope will happen after people laugh?
A play shows a politician who promises 'free electricity for all' while selling the town's transformer. This is an example of:
The play mocks the politician's empty promises and corruption. That is satire.
Is the writer praising or criticising him?
Which device is most often used in satire?
Satire relies on irony, exaggeration and ridicule.
How does a writer make wrongdoing look foolish?
Exaggerating a person's features or habits to mock them
A caricature exaggerates traits to make the target look ridiculous.
Think of cartoons of politicians in newspapers.
How is satire related to irony?
Satire is the aim of ridiculing vice; irony is one of the tools it uses
Satire is a type of rhyme
Irony is always longer than satire
Satire is the overall purpose and mode; irony is a technique that helps achieve it.
Which is the goal and which is the tool?
A newspaper cartoon shows a giant 'Minister of Roads' in a jeep floating over potholes full of water. What is the cartoonist satirising?
The cartoon mocks officials who don't feel the problems of ordinary road users.
Gentle, amused satire that laughs at human weaknesses is called:
Horatian satire is light and humorous. Juvenalian satire is harsh and angry.
There are two main kinds: one gentle, one bitter.
Bitter, angry satire that attacks serious evils is called:
Juvenalian satire is harsh and condemns serious wrongdoing with anger.
lit-u4-l5: Socratic irony is when a character:
Pretends to be ignorant in order to expose another person's ignorance or guilt
Speaks alone on stage
Mourns the dead
Says exactly what he means
Feigned ignorance draws the other person out, revealing their weakness.
Does the character really not know?
An old woman asks the chairman, 'Please, I'm only a village woman. Can you explain how the borehole money disappeared?' What is she doing?
Using feigned ignorance to expose his corruption
Asking a real question out of curiosity
Praising the chairman
Telling a folktale
She pretends to be simple so that he has to explain, and his explanation exposes him.
Does she really not know where the money went?
Which word best describes the tone of Socratic irony?
Mocking innocence
Open anger
Pure sadness
Simple joy
The speaker appears innocent but is quietly mocking the other person.
Is the innocence real?
Why is Socratic irony effective against powerful characters?
It makes them reveal their own faults without being openly attacked
It makes them stronger
It praises them
It hides the truth forever
Innocent-seeming questions trap the powerful into exposing themselves.
Who does the revealing: the questioner or the answerer?
Socratic irony is named after Socrates because he:
Pretended not to know answers in order to question others' beliefs
Wrote many plays
Was a king
Invented rhyme
Socrates, the Greek philosopher, questioned people while claiming ignorance.
How did Socrates teach?
A student asks the teacher who keeps coming late: 'Sir, what time does class start? I forgot.' What device might the student be using?
Socratic irony
Onomatopoeia
Alliteration
Metonymy
The student pretends not to know in order to hint at the teacher's lateness.
Did the student really forget?
Which of these is NOT a feature of Socratic irony?
The speaker openly insults the other person
The speaker pretends to be ignorant
The speaker asks questions
The other person exposes himself
Socratic irony works indirectly; open insult is not part of it.
Is Socratic irony direct or indirect?
In satire, Socratic irony often helps a writer to:
Expose corruption through innocent-seeming questions
Describe landscapes
Write rhyming verses
Tell the history of a town
Feigned ignorance is a satirical tool for exposing those in power.
How does it help criticism?
After hearing a liar's story, an elder says, 'My son, I am an old man, I do not understand. Please tell me again slowly.' The elder most likely wants to:
Make the liar repeat the story until its holes show
Learn a new song
Fall asleep
Praise the liar
Asking him to repeat it gives the liar room to contradict himself. That is Socratic irony.
Why ask a liar to repeat his story?
lit-u5-l1: A soliloquy is:
A speech where a character alone on stage speaks his thoughts aloud
A conversation between two characters
A song by the chorus
A stage direction
In a soliloquy the character, usually alone, reveals inner thoughts to the audience.
'Solo' means alone.
What is the main purpose of a soliloquy?
To reveal a character's private thoughts and feelings
To introduce comic relief
To change the setting
To end the play
Soliloquies let the audience into a character's mind.
What can the audience learn that other characters cannot?
How is a soliloquy different from a monologue?
A soliloquy is spoken alone to oneself; a monologue is a long speech that may be addressed to others
They are the same thing
A monologue is always sung
A soliloquy involves many characters
Both are long speeches, but a soliloquy is private, while a monologue can be addressed to listeners.
Is anyone else listening?
In Shakespeare's Hamlet, 'To be or not to be' is spoken by Hamlet alone. This is an example of:
A soliloquy
An aside
Comic relief
A chorus
Hamlet speaks his inner thoughts alone, which makes it a soliloquy.
Is he alone when he speaks?
A soliloquy can create dramatic irony because:
The audience learns secrets that other characters do not know
It is always funny
It ends the play
It is spoken by the chorus
Once the audience hears a character's secret plans, it knows more than the others on stage.
What do we know after hearing it?
A villain explains his evil plan in a soliloquy. How does this affect the audience?
They feel suspense as they wait to see the plan unfold
They become confused
They forget the plot
They feel nothing
Knowing the plan creates suspense and tension.
How do you feel knowing a secret plan?
Which stage situation best suits a soliloquy?
A worried character alone at night thinking aloud
A crowded market scene
A fight between two soldiers
A wedding dance
A soliloquy needs a character alone, expressing private thoughts.
Who should be on stage?
What should a student mention when analysing a soliloquy?
What it reveals about the character's mind and how it affects the plot
Only how long it is
The colour of the costume
The rhyme scheme only
Focus on what we learn about the character and how it shapes events.
What does it tell us, and why does it matter?
A character in a Nigerian play speaks alone about whether to accept a bribe. The soliloquy mainly shows:
His inner conflict
The setting of the play
The comic side of the story
The ending of the play
Debating with himself reveals his inner moral struggle.
What is he struggling with inside?
lit-u5-l2: A short remark spoken to the audience that other characters on stage do not hear
A long speech made alone on stage
An aside is a brief comment heard by the audience but not by the other characters.
What is the main difference between an aside and a soliloquy?
An aside is short and other characters are present; a soliloquy is longer and usually spoken alone
A soliloquy is heard by all characters
An aside is a quick remark with others on stage. A soliloquy is a longer private speech.
Think about length and who is on stage.
During a meeting, a character says to the audience, '(Aside) If they only knew I stole the money.' What does this create?
The audience now knows his secret, which the others don't. That is dramatic irony.
How is an aside usually shown in a play script?
Playwrights mark it with '(Aside)' so actors know to speak it to the audience.
Why might a playwright use an aside in a comedy?
To let a character share a joke or secret with the audience
Asides create a bond between character and audience, often for humour.
How does it involve the audience?
A suitor smiles at the bride's father and says, '(Aside) This old man must not discover my debts.' What does the aside reveal?
The suitor is hiding his debts and is not honest
The aside shows the suitor's hidden worry and dishonesty.
Reveal hidden thoughts quickly without stopping the scene
A quick aside shares inner thoughts while the action goes on.
Does the scene stop for an aside?
Which of these is an aside?
(Aside) I must get that land, by fair means or foul.
The '(Aside)' line is a remark meant only for the audience.
Which line is marked as spoken only to the audience?
In an aside, the other characters on stage:
Are understood not to hear the remark
By stage convention the other characters do not hear an aside.
It's a stage convention. What do they pretend?
lit-u5-l3: Comic relief is:
A humorous scene or character placed in a serious play to ease tension
The happy ending of a tragedy
A sad song
A stage direction
Comic relief adds humour to give the audience a break from tension.
What do we need after an intense scene?
In a tragedy, why might a playwright include a funny scene with two drunk guards?
To give the audience relief before the tension rises again
To make the play a comedy
To confuse the audience
To introduce the hero
A moment of laughter relieves tension and makes the next serious scene stronger.
How does laughter change the mood?
Comic relief can also help to:
Highlight the seriousness of the main events by contrast
Remove the main theme
End the play early
Replace the plot
The contrast with humour makes the tragic scenes feel even heavier.
What happens when light sits beside dark?
Which character is most likely to provide comic relief?
A talkative, foolish servant
A grieving widow
A dying king
A wise priest giving a warning
Foolish servants, jesters and clowns often supply comic relief.
Who makes the audience laugh?
The porter scene in Shakespeare's Macbeth comes right after the murder of the king. Its function is:
Comic relief
Foreshadowing
Climax
Resolution
The drunk porter's jokes relieve the horror of the murder for a moment.
How does a drunk man joking after a murder affect the audience?
Which of these best describes the effect of comic relief?
It releases tension and keeps the audience engaged
It makes the audience leave
It explains the plot
It shows the setting
Laughter refreshes the audience and keeps their attention.
Why don't tragedies stay tense the whole time?
In a Nigerian play about a land dispute, a gossiping palm-wine tapper jokes between tense court scenes. He mainly serves as:
Comic relief
The protagonist
The antagonist
The narrator
His jokes lighten the mood between serious scenes.
What does his humour do to the tension?
Comic relief is most commonly found in:
Tragedies and serious dramas
Dictionaries
News reports
Science textbooks
Comic relief balances serious drama, especially tragedy.
Where is relief needed most?
What should you avoid saying about comic relief in an exam?
That it has no purpose in the play
That it eases tension
That it creates contrast
That it keeps the audience engaged
Comic relief always has a purpose, so saying it has none is wrong.
Which option goes against its function?
lit-u5-l4: A hint or clue about what will happen later in the story
Foreshadowing gives early hints of later events.
Early in a novel, dark clouds gather on the wedding day. This most likely foreshadows:
Dark clouds are a warning sign, hinting at trouble ahead.
What do dark clouds usually signal?
A character says, 'I have a strange feeling I won't return from this journey.' This line is an example of:
The remark hints that something bad may happen on the journey.
Is it hinting at the future?
What is the main effect of foreshadowing?
It builds suspense and prepares the reader for later events
Hints make readers anticipate and wonder what will happen.
How do you feel when you sense something is coming?
How is foreshadowing different from flashback?
Foreshadowing hints at the future; flashback goes back to the past
Foreshadowing points forward and flashback points back.
One looks ahead, the other looks back.
In a play, a soothsayer warns the king to beware of his own household. Later his son betrays him. The warning was:
The early warning hinted at the later betrayal.
When did the warning come, before or after?
'A gun shown in the first act should be fired by the last.' This saying is about:
Foreshadowing: details introduced early should matter later
Chekhov's idea is that early details should pay off later in the story.
Why show a gun at the start?
Which of these is most likely foreshadowing in a story?
A broken mirror on the morning of a big journey
A broken mirror is a traditional bad omen, hinting at misfortune ahead.
Which detail feels like a warning?
When writing about foreshadowing in an exam, you should:
Identify the early hint and link it to the later event it points to
Show the hint, then explain how it connects to what happens later.
Connect the clue to its result.
lit-u5-l5: The moment when a character recognises the truth about his situation
Anagnorisis is the moment of discovery or recognition, often in tragedy.
Peripeteia is the turn where the hero's fortune changes, often from good to bad.
Think of the moment things turn around.
The tragic flaw or error that leads to the hero's downfall
Hamartia is the flaw or mistake, such as pride, that brings the hero down.
Excessive pride that often leads to a tragic hero's fall
Hubris is arrogant pride and is a common tragic flaw.
Think of a proud king who defies the gods.
Catharsis is the feeling the audience experiences when:
Their pity and fear are released at the end of a tragedy
Aristotle described catharsis as the emotional cleansing felt after a tragedy.
How do you feel after watching a sad ending?
In The Gods Are Not to Blame, Odewale's quick temper and pride contribute to his downfall. These qualities are his:
His temper and pride are flaws that lead to his tragic actions.
A person of high status with a flaw that leads to his fall
A villain with no good qualities
Classical tragic heroes are noble but flawed, and their fall stirs pity.
Why do we pity a tragic hero?
When a king discovers that the stranger he killed years ago was his own father, this moment is:
It is the moment of terrible recognition, which is anagnorisis.
What does the king suddenly discover?
Which order best matches a typical tragic pattern?
The flaw causes errors, fortune reverses, the hero recognises the truth, and he falls.
What has to come first for the rest to happen?
lit-u6-l1: The persona in a poem is:
The speaker or voice created by the poet
Always the poet himself
The title of the poem
The rhyme scheme
The persona is the voice speaking in the poem, which may differ from the poet.
Is the 'I' in a poem always the poet?
A poem written by a man begins: 'As a mother of five, I wake before the cock crows.' Who is the persona?
A mother of five
The poet
The cock
The reader
The speaker is a mother of five, a voice the poet has created.
Who is speaking in the poem?
Why do poets create a persona?
To express experiences or views from a different perspective
To hide the title
To make the poem rhyme
To shorten the poem
A persona lets the poet speak through another person's eyes.
What can a poet gain by speaking as someone else?
In an exam, the question 'Who is the speaker?' asks you to identify:
The persona and what we learn about them from the poem
The poet's real name and date of birth
The publisher
The number of stanzas
Describe the persona using clues from the poem.
Use evidence from the poem.
A poem begins: 'I am the river. I have carried canoes for a thousand years.' The persona is:
The river
A fisherman
The poet only
A canoe
The speaker is the river itself, which is also personification.
Who says 'I am'?
Which clue best helps you identify the persona of a poem?
The words, experiences and attitudes the speaker expresses
The colour of the book cover
The page number
The font size
The speaker's language and experiences reveal who they are.
Look at what the speaker says and feels.
A poem says: 'I sold my school uniform for bread.' What does this suggest about the persona?
A young person in deep poverty
A rich trader
A teacher on holiday
A tailor
Selling a uniform for bread suggests a poor young student.
Who wears a school uniform, and why would they sell it?
Point of view in a poem refers to:
The perspective from which the poem is told
The poem's rhythm
The poem's length
The time it was written
Point of view is the position of the speaker, such as first person 'I' or third person.
From whose eyes do we see?
A poem uses 'he' and 'she' to describe others rather than 'I'. The point of view is:
Third person
First person
Second person
No point of view
Using 'he', 'she' and 'they' to describe others is a third-person point of view.
Is the speaker talking about himself or others?
lit-u6-l2: The speaker's attitude towards the subject
Tone is the speaker's attitude, such as angry, sad or mocking.
The feeling or atmosphere created for the reader
Mood is the atmosphere the reader feels, such as gloomy or joyful.
How does the poem make YOU feel?
A poem says: 'Our leaders feast while children starve.' The tone is best described as:
The contrast between feasting and starving shows anger at the leaders.
How does the speaker feel about the leaders?
Which words help a reader identify tone?
The poet's word choice (diction) and imagery
Diction and imagery reveal attitude: harsh words suggest anger, soft words suggest tenderness.
Look closely at the words chosen.
A poem describes 'grey rain, empty streets, and a silent drum'. The mood is:
Grey rain, emptiness and silence create a gloomy, sad atmosphere.
What feeling do these images create?
A poem mocks a man who brags about his wealth while owing everyone money. The tone is:
Mocking someone's foolishness shows a satirical tone.
Is the speaker serious or mocking?
Which of these is a TONE word?
'Sarcastic' describes attitude. The others are features of form.
A poem describes children dancing in the rain during harvest. The mood is most likely:
Dancing children and harvest suggest celebration and joy.
What do dancing and harvest suggest?
Why is it important to quote evidence when describing tone in an exam?
It proves your claim using the poet's own words
Quotations support your reading of the tone.
How do you prove what you say?
lit-u6-l3: A shift in tone in a poem means:
The speaker's attitude changes at some point
The poem changes its title
The poet changes
The poem changes language
A tonal shift is a change in the speaker's attitude, often marked by a turning word.
What changes: the attitude or the poet?
Which word often signals a shift in a poem?
But
And
The
Of
Words like 'but', 'yet' and 'however' often introduce a contrast or change.
Which word introduces a contrast?
A poem praises a city's bright lights, then says: 'Yet beneath the bridge, a child sleeps hungry.' The shift is from:
Admiration to concern
Sadness to joy
Anger to humour
Fear to excitement
'Yet' turns the praise into concern for the poor child.
What does the speaker feel before and after 'Yet'?
Why do poets use a turn or shift?
To create contrast and deepen the meaning
To confuse the reader
To end the poem early
To fill space
A shift can reveal complexity, surprise the reader, or make a point through contrast.
What does contrast do to meaning?
In a sonnet, the turn in thought is called the:
Volta
Refrain
Couplet only
Caesura
The volta is the turn in argument or mood in a sonnet.
It's an Italian word for 'turn'.
A poem moves from 'The drums were loud, the dancers proud' to 'Now the compound is silent, the drums are cold.' The shift suggests:
A change from celebration to loss
A change from sadness to joy
No change
Humour
The silence and cold drums suggest that celebration has given way to grief.
What do silent drums suggest?
When writing about a shift, a good answer should:
Identify where the shift happens and explain how the tone changes
Only say that the poem is long
Give the poet's biography
Copy the whole poem
Point to the exact turning point and describe the before-and-after tone.
Where does it happen, and what changes?
A poem's first stanza describes a mother's hopes for her son; the last stanza describes his grave. The structure creates:
A tragic contrast between hope and loss
Comic relief
A happy ending
A rhyme scheme
Setting hope beside death creates a powerful tragic contrast.
Put the first and last stanzas side by side.
Which of these lines contains a turn word that signals a contrast?
The harvest was rich; however, the farmer wept.
The harvest was rich and the farmer smiled.
The farmer harvested yams.
The farmer sold yams at the market.
'However' signals a contrast between the rich harvest and the weeping farmer.
Find the word that introduces a contrast.
lit-u6-l4: A Shakespearean (English) sonnet has how many lines?
What is the rhyme scheme of a Shakespearean sonnet?
It has three quatrains with alternate rhyme and a closing rhyming couplet.
It ends with a couplet: GG.
A Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet is divided into:
An octave (8 lines) and a sestet (6 lines)
The Petrarchan sonnet has an eight-line octave and a six-line sestet.
The final couplet of a Shakespearean sonnet usually:
Sums up the poem or gives a twist
The closing couplet often resolves the argument or surprises the reader.
What do the last two lines often do?
A quatrain is a stanza of:
'Quatr' means four, so a quatrain has four lines.
A couplet is a pair of lines, usually rhyming.
A sonnet that praises harmattan mornings for twelve lines and then ends with 'Yet dust has choked my mother's ailing breath' uses the couplet to:
Undercut the praise with a painful twist
The final lines turn praise into pain, a typical twist in the couplet.
How do the last lines change the poem?
Iambic pentameter, the usual metre of English sonnets, has:
Ten syllables per line in five unstressed-stressed pairs
Iambic pentameter has five iambs (da-DUM) per line, which makes ten syllables.
A 14-line lyric poem with a set rhyme scheme
A long story of a hero
A sonnet is a 14-line lyric with a fixed rhyme pattern.
